extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers and graduate students) writing, publishing, and disseminating mathematical work online
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians on preparing, submitting, archiving, and disseminating mathematical writing in the digital era, covering figures, hypertext, electronic journals, preprint servers (arXiv), indexing (MathSciNet), blogs, wikis, and social media. Emphasizes practical workflows, formats, copyright, and collaboration tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper tools for figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the proper tools in the proper context (e.g., hand-drawing a rectangle or triangle may take five minutes but graphing a function could take hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spend hours trying to hand-draw complex figures; instead draw simple shapes by hand if appropriate, but for production-quality or time-saving rendering use vector graphics tools such as Corel DRAW! or Adobe Illustrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext linking to cognate items
rubrics_metrics.description: With hypertext, accented words or phrases can be clicked to jump to a definition, a lexicon, a menu of options, or to the text of a reference or an author's home page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypertext to let readers jump to definitions (e.g., 'pseudoconvex'), references, related papers, author pages, or animated graphics—this bypasses flipping through printed material and leverages the web's navigational strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing bypasses hard copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publishing aims to bypass traditional hard copy and make materials available on the Internet and the World Wide Web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for transactions (submission, refereeing, editorial decision, publication) to be executed online; consider how identification, access control, payment, and archiving will be handled in an electronic environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic journals often eliminate issues/volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: One interesting feature of all-electronic journals is that they make the notion of an 'issue' or a 'volume' passé; papers can be published sequentially rather than in batches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect continuous publication models rather than traditional batched issues; plan timelines and citations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Access (OA) principle and flavors
rubrics_metrics.description: Open Access: anyone can read the articles without paying for a subscription. Flavors: 'gold' OA (delivered by journals), 'green' OA (delivered by repositories), and 'libre' OA (removing permissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the OA model you choose: authors may pay substantial fees (often thousands of dollars) for journal-based OA; repositories may avoid fees but have other policies. Evaluate financial and accessibility implications before choosing venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate OA fees and publisher incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: If a commercial publisher chooses to publish an OA journal then someone has to pay the publisher’s expenses, so a fee is levied against the author; proponents hope models will shift from subscription to author-fee funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether you or your institution/grant can pay author fees; be aware of predatory/dishonest publishers who may accept substandard papers to generate income; weigh reputational and archival consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival/disaster-backup responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers or organizations (e.g., AMS) may make archival/disaster-backup copies of electronic journals as a service to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer journals or platforms that commit to archiving/backups; consider the permanence of the venue when choosing where to post work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic journals: page limitations and article length
rubrics_metrics.description: With an electronic journal, page limitations are not important; therefore an electronic journal can publish longer articles and more of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume strict page-count constraints for electronic-only venues, but be mindful of readability and editorial norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic submission/workflow and output formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic journals generally transact submission, referee reports, editorial decisions, and publication by e-mail; published papers are posted in output formats such as *.dvi, *.eps, or *.pdf and there are no reprints or hard copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to submit source and output files electronically; know which output formats the journal uses and whether they provide compiled output or require you to supply it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of CD-ROM or downloadable hard copy for archival use
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, CD-ROM versions of the electronic journal are available for archival purposes; usually end users can download individual papers for compiling and hard copy printing for personal use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If long-term offline archiving matters for you or your institution, inquire about CD-ROM/archive options and download policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous electronic and hard-copy publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hard-copy journals simultaneously publish an electronic version and may make accepted papers available electronically for a modest charge as soon as the paper is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check a journal's policy about early electronic availability, simultaneous publication, and any fees associated with immediate electronic access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of electronic-only journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages include: no shelf space, cannot be lost or stolen, unlimited simultaneous access, and the ability for users to print their own hard copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these advantages to improve distribution and accessibility, but balance them against archiving and quality-control concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of copyright law in electronic publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The copyright law issues connected with electronic publishing are immense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the copyright implications of posting online (arXiv, personal webpages) and of signing journal copyright transfer agreements; negotiate retained rights when possible if you want future reuse flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers may suggest web ancillaries and interactive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publishers propose that a home page be set up for a book and that ancillaries (relevant papers, bibliographic database, exercise books, lecture manuals) appear on the Web site; in some scenarios readers may contribute interactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider creating or accepting web ancillaries to enhance a book/paper, but plan for maintenance, moderation, and rights management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative writing workflow by email
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative mathematical work via e-mail: send source (ourpaper.tex) as e-mail attachments—usually both a *.tex file and a *.pdf file—and retain the master copy on your system's hard disk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use email attachments for quick collaboration; send both source and compiled output; maintain a single authoritative master copy and version-control practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX comments for in-document collaborative notes
rubrics_metrics.description: If you type comments in the TeX document and precede each line with a % symbol, TeX will ignore those lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate source files with % comments for collaborator notes and instructions that won't appear in the compiled document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of platform/file-format interoperability
rubrics_metrics.description: There are differences in the ways files are formatted on microcomputers versus UNIX systems; consult local support for uploading and transferring files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moving files between home PCs/Macs and university UNIX systems, watch for line endings, encoding, and path/filename conventions; consider using platform-compatible tools (e.g., Linux) or transfer utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint servers are unrefereed repositories
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper posted on a preprint server is not refereed or vetted in any way; it is just posted for all the world to see and anyone can view/download/print posted papers (arXiv has an entry level for submission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preprint servers to disseminate results quickly, but recognize they are not substitutes for peer review and vetting; state clearly the status of a preprint when publicizing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv accepts only TeX/LaTeX sources and compiles them
rubrics_metrics.description: An interesting feature of arXiv is that it only accepts TeX submissions (raw TeX or LaTeX); arXiv compiles your paper on the spot—if it succeeds you may proceed; if it fails your submission stops. arXiv prefers LaTeX2e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make TeX files self-contained, prefer LaTeX2e, test compilation locally before submission, and address any package or class dependencies to avoid arXiv compilation failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing graphics and separate files for arXiv
rubrics_metrics.description: If your paper has separate graphics files, it may be tricky to get arXiv to compile and accept your paper, but it can be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure graphics are present, in accepted formats, and referenced correctly; consider consolidating figures where possible or providing source and accompanying files per arXiv guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and communicate a definitive version
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you write something there may be many versions floating around (multiple local copies, arXiv, home page); which is the definitive version is not always clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a personal policy to identify and communicate the authoritative version (e.g., arXiv version x.y, journal published version) to collaborators and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand publisher policies on retained rights and preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may grant the author non-exclusive rights to reproduce and distribute certain versions (preprint, accepted manuscript) for scholarly purposes; some policies are more or less permissive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read publisher policies carefully, negotiate retained rights if you want reuse permission, and keep copies of retained-rights clauses when signing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arXiv front-ends for better usability
rubrics_metrics.description: Front (front.math.ucdavis.edu) is a user-friendly front end for arXiv that makes arXiv easier to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using community-built front-ends and tools to search, browse, and receive notifications from arXiv more conveniently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MathSciNet for bibliographic and author identification
rubrics_metrics.description: MathSciNet provides author identification (disambiguation), searches by many fields, BibTeX entries, MathJax linking, and metrics like number of papers, citations, and principal collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master MathSciNet for compiling bibliographies, tracking citations, disambiguating authors, and exploring collaboration distances; use provided BibTeX entries to ease reference management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blogs as informal, interactive dissemination venues
rubrics_metrics.description: A blog is an informational website of discrete, often informal posts (reverse chronological); modern blogs are often interactive and multi-author, allowing comments and social interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blogs for rapid informal communication, teaching notes, problem discussions, and outreach; recognize they typically lack refereeing and that contributions may be public and editable via comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chat rooms and synchronous collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Chat rooms are used for synchronous conferencing to share information via text with a group; they may include file sharing and webcam features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chat rooms for real-time collaboration and discussion; choose synchronous tools (Skype, FaceTime, chat rooms) when instant back-and-forth or live demonstrations are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikis for collaborative authored content
rubrics_metrics.description: A wiki provides collaborative modification of content from the browser; text is usually written in simplified markup and is editable by many users (e.g., Wikipedia, WikiMath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribute to wikis for shared educational resources or living documents, but expect that content is collaboratively edited and individual authorship may not be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan attribution, authorship, and funding for large collaborative efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: If many people contribute to a mathematical result (e.g., via a blog or polymath), questions arise: who writes it up, whose name goes on the paper, where to submit, who pays author fees for OA journals?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before large-scale collaboration, agree on authorship rules, write-up responsibilities, venue selection, and how any publication costs will be handled to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media characteristics and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media are interactive Web 2.0 applications where user-generated content (text posts, comments, photos, videos) is the lifeblood; they foster networking, outreach, and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media for outreach, advertising results, and community engagement, but be mindful of audience, tone, permanence, and the difference between social media and scholarly publishing.
